task: Write one sentence of your own using the word querulous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know querulous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The querulous carpool rider found the seat too far forward, the radio too loud, and the shortcut 'suspicious.'
Dissatisfied stops far short of querulous — dissatisfaction is the quiet feeling before any complaint is spoken.
Peevish stops short of querulous — the peevish are irritable in the moment, while the querulous keep a running list of grievances aloud.

Carping means continually picking at faults — the carping critic nags about every flaw as though grading it. Querulous complains just as constantly but in a whinier key: the querulous voice sounds aggrieved and put-upon rather than sharp. Carping attacks the work in front of it; querulous laments the whole arrangement of the world.

Whiny is the informal word for the complaining tone itself — high, drawn-out, childish. Querulous is its dressed-up cousin and claims more: not one complaint's sound but the settled habit of producing them, a running commentary of grievances. A toddler is whiny for an afternoon; a querulous tenant files notes for years.

Querulous means habitually complaining.

The building's querulous tenant slips a note under the superintendent's door most mornings: the elevator hums in E-flat, the lobby ferns 'stare,' the new doormat is 'aggressively beige.' The super files them all in a shoebox marked 'weather.'
Querulous describes a habit, not a mood: anyone can grumble on a bad day, but the querulous complain as a running commentary, finding a fresh grievance in every arrangement.
Querulous is for the standing habit of complaint — the voice that finds a grievance in every arrangement.
One-off grumbling is just 'grumpy.' Its unit-mate obstreperous makes trouble at the opposite volume: roaring against control rather than whining about it.

The Gazette's archivist knew Colonel Petty's envelopes by the handwriting alone.
For nineteen years he had written weekly: the town's benches were too low, the church bells a half-tone flat, the new stamps disrespectful, the weather reports optimistic to the point of mockery.
The letters were never angry, exactly.
Their tone was querulous — wounded, put-upon, as though the town had arranged each inconvenience with the colonel personally in mind.
Editors came and went; the letters did not.
When the paper finally printed one under the heading 'A Reader Suffers,' the colonel wrote to complain about the heading — and, in a postscript, about the font.
